second_order: moving pixel work to Discord and pxls.space
theme_note: These codes move pixel-making beyond the subreddit: first to Discord for detailed Ness coordination. The later slice extends the same practice to continuing on a successor canvas.

second_order: calling people in to build the next character or mark
theme_note: These codes recruit others into making the display larger. What varies is the proposed object—characters, logos, marks, details, or a later crossover—not the practice of proposing the next addition and asking people to join.

second_order: laying out coordinates, borders, backgrounds, and build order
theme_note: These codes make pixel work executable by locating it, defining edges and fills, choosing backdrops, redirecting planning, or specifying an order of work. They range from rough spatial cues to measured rectangles and strict row order.

second_order: defending, rebuilding, and maintaining threatened art
theme_note: These codes treat a supposedly finished image as ongoing work: maintaining it, reporting damage, replacing pixels, rallying defenders, or renewing a fight. The threats vary from trolls and griefing to the taskbar, while the shared practice is keeping threatened art standing.

second_order: working things out with neighbours and the taskbar
theme_note: These codes manage coexistence with surrounding builders through borders, aid, exchanges, camouflage, respect, mutual watching, and compromise. Some seek partnership and others accept losses; what holds them together is working out how EarthBound art can remain among other projects.

second_order: making the subreddit’s own April Fools jokes
theme_note: These codes perform or recognize the community's separate April Fools conduct: fake releases and streams, a renamed Discord, borrowed meme formats, a joke video, and a Starman punchline. They are not canvas work even when they occur beside it.

second_order: joking in EarthBound language about canvas trouble
theme_note: These codes turn the canvas and its damage into EarthBound talk—Master Belch, an injured Lucas, and jokes on the event's name. Unlike the subreddit’s own April Fools pranks, these jokes are ways of talking about the shared canvas.

second_order: celebrating finished work and thanking helpers
theme_note: This slice first marks a made-and-surviving Mr. Saturn; the later slice extends the practice through public closure, beauty, gratitude, participation, and shout-outs.

second_order: gathering crowded suggestions into one megathread
theme_note: These two codes centralize many small suggestion threads and establish how the combined thread will be ordered and moderated. This is a single final-slice practice rather than a general label for coordination.

second_order: remembering the work and one’s part in it
theme_note: These codes look back on making and defending the display by recalling added figures, late contributions, lost sleep, temporary success, first builds, and a favorite part. The claims vary in scale, but each places effort or participation into the shared account.

second_order: mourning missing pieces while valuing what survived
theme_note: These codes inventory angry eyebrows, missing noses, erased cultists, and all-day repair while taking consolation in surviving cultists and Mr. Saturns. Loss and appreciation occur together rather than forming separate practices.

These codes trace whether removed pixels produced the banner error, publicly repeat it as EarthCound, and come to love it. They hold together as participants turn a defect into an affectionate name, not merely because they share the same word.

second_order: explaining r/place to people who missed it
theme_note: These codes answer newcomers and returning visitors by explaining the pixel canvas, the cooperation among subreddits, and what EarthBound participants fought for and made. The questions differ, while the practice is making the event legible after the fact.
